nameStory: Long-leaved Redtop-Panicgrass gets its name from its notably elongated leaves and the reddish-tinged flower clusters that form a loose, branching pattern called a panicle. The 'redtop' part refers to how the seed heads often take on rusty or purplish hues as they mature, creating colorful patches in late summer grasslands.
description: Long-leaved Redtop-Panicgrass is a native perennial grass that forms small clumps or grows as individual stems. It typically reaches 2-4 feet tall with distinctively long, narrow leaves that give it its common name. The plant produces loose, open clusters of tiny flowers that later develop into small seeds, and it's considered quite rare in New England with only a handful of known locations.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Notably long and narrow leaves that feel smooth to the touch, typically 6-12 inches long but only about a quarter-inch wide, giving the plant an elegant, flowing appearance

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Loose, open clusters of tiny flowers that start green but often develop reddish or purplish tints, branching in an airy pattern above the leaves in late summer

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small clumps or grows as scattered individual stems, typically 2-4 feet tall, with an upright but graceful posture that sways gently in breezes

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, oval seeds that are barely an eighth of an inch long, held in loose clusters that create a delicate, almost lacy appearance

habitat: Long-leaved Redtop-Panicgrass prefers sandy or well-drained soils in open areas like prairies, woodland edges, and disturbed sites. It's typically found in sunny to partially shaded locations and may grow alongside other native grasses and wildflowers in remnant grassland habitats.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from the base, with the characteristic long leaves beginning to unfurl and establish the plant's distinctive appearance.
seasonality.summer: Leaves reach full length and the plant achieves its mature height, with flower clusters beginning to develop in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Flower heads mature and take on their reddish colors, with seeds ripening and dispersing. Leaves may begin to yellow or turn brown.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back, leaving only dried stems and seed heads that may persist into early winter before breaking down.

funFact: This grass is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only 6 times by naturalists and botanists, making it rarer than finding a four-leaf clover - if you encounter it, you're looking at one of the region's most elusive native plants!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other native bunch grasses, but the exceptionally long, narrow leaves are the key distinguishing feature - if the leaves look almost ribbon-like and seem unusually long for the plant's height, you've likely found Long-leaved Redtop-Panicgrass.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name recently changed from Panicum to Coleataenia as botanists better understood grass relationships through genetic studies, so you might see this plant listed under different names in older field guides.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative Redtop Panicgrass, Long-leaved Redtop-Panicgrass has distinctly longer and narrower leaves that are more ribbon-like in appearance. While both species can develop reddish flower clusters, the leaf length difference is usually obvious when the two are compared side by side.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Long-leaved redtop panicgrass (Coleataenia longifolia) is taller and has longer, wider leaves as its name suggests, typically growing 3-5 feet tall compared to redtop panicgrass's 2-4 feet.
